Hon, W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture): My attention has been called by the Prime Minister to a question that was asked yesterday by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Elliott) with respect to the Shire horses that have recently arrived from Great Britain and are now stationed at the Experimental Farm here. The question was asked as to the disposition of these breeding animals throughout Canada. Our natural desire, Mr. Speaker, is to place these animals in conformity with the wishes of the donors, since they have been made a gift by the Shire Breeders' Society of Great Britain. It is equally our natural desire to place them where some attention has already been given to the breeding of Shire horses, and we find on examining our records that the two places that have paid the most attention to the breeding of Shire horses are Lacombe in the province of Alberta and Len-noxville in the province of Quebec. There are very few, however, in the latter place, consequently it was thought that for the best use of these breeding animals and to carry out the wishes of the donors it would be wise to locate them in Alberta, at Lacombe. This, however, is only a tentative arrangement and the final disposition of the horses will not be made until the return of Mr. Archibald, Director of the Dominion Experimental Farms, who will return on Monday or Tuesday next. In the meantime we shall be very glad to have any representations from Ontario or elsewhere as to where these animals could be placed to better advantage than under the arrangement already made.
So far as locating them in Ontario is concerned, there are a few Shire horses scattered here and there throughout the province, but we have had no intimation from any source that they would like to have the Shires mixed with other breeds here.

I had the pleasure of
examining these horses to-day and they

A few trivial things in connection with our manufactured products-and they are spare parts at that-are reduced. They are wortn while, but relatively they are trifles. Let us have it established in our minds that we have a higher tariff against us for Canadian exports to France than we had before, and that for our agricultural exports to France- and this is very important when we are speaking about wider markets-we are getting by this treaty, a narrower market that we had before. Nobody can dispute that in the frankness and serenity of his own mind. He may say, as an hon. member said last night, that is a departure from rectitude to refer to that. I do not so regard it, and I do not regard that remark as worth answering. In the next place, we have a lower tariff than we had before on luxuries imported into Canada. Of that there can be no doubt, and it is not worth while arguing to establish that. I ask another thing to be considered,
that if we had been free to increase our tariff on luxuries and the French government knew we were free-I mean on the goods on which they have now a lower tariff -then we would have beqn on an equality or better than an equality in the negotiations with France; because, aside from war years and the immediately subsequent years, if you look back over all the normal years of our history, French exports to us are about five times ours to France-they average almost five times for the five years preceding the war. Have I made that premise clear, that had we been free to exercise the weapon that was in the hands of France, we woidd have been on more than an equality in the negotiations? I do not ask that to be conceded, I do ask it to be conceded that we would have been on an equality. These things nobody can dispute at all; First, we have a higher tariff against our exports to France than we had before, chiefly as regards agr-cultural exports; second,, we have a lower tariff against imports of luxuries into Canada ; and third, had we been free, aside wholly from the history of our politics, to have used France's weapon on the goods France sent to us, we would have been on at least an equality with the French negotiators. If those are conceded, let me put the matter in this form. Leave out of account the history of the Liberal party and the history of the Conservative party, and assume that bound by nothing and considering the interest of Canada and nothing else, our negotiators went to France. Did they not have to choose between two things: first, a higher tariff against luxuries into Canada and a lower tariff against agricultural products into France, or, on the other hand, a lower tariff against luxuries into Canada and a higher tariff against agricultural products into France? Which would they have chosen, had there been no commitments and no political history to tie their hands? There is not a man at large in this country who would not choose the higher tariff on luxuries coming into Canada and a lower tariff on agricultural products going into France. Then why have we not that? Had there been no political history in this matter, we should have had it; had there been no political commitments that would have been the state of affairs. And we have not got it just because of those commitments. That is all I want hon. gentlemen to admit; and while I do not expect them to admit it aloud, it is nevertheless the truth. If hon. gentlemen opposite think the matter over they cannot help being convinced that this is the fact.

And therein is a lesson. This is one of the products of wrong pre-election commitments and principles. I know there are other products, of course; another product we had last session when there was a violation of those commitments,-a very bad harvest indeed. We have not the same consequences to-day; we have to-day another product of false political commitments, not as bad morally but financially worse; the harvest this time is the sacrifice of Canadian interests. And while you may have it in one form or the other, you are bound to reap a harvest of ill if you make commitments that are false. This is one product of such a policy; as I have stated, last session we had another. And these are not, the last. Now, I have stated in very brief form the way I sincerely view the whole history of this French treaty negotiation; and this government in other negotiations must either abandon and prostitute its principles or sacrifice the interests of Canada. Last session it chose the first; this session it chooses the second.

My right hon. friend knows that the existing rates are as dead as Julius Caesar. Why then does he compare the live body of this treaty with the dead corpse of that old arrangement? Does the right hon. gentleman not know that the present condition which he speaks of, and which he compares with the rates as set forth in the French treaty, cannot be taken advantage of now? Again and again we are told that this treaty is not as good as the old one; but my right hon. friend knows that the French government gave definite notice abrogating the old one. He knows also that after certain negotiations, succeeding the termination of the old treaty, an interim arrangement

was made-and made by himself and his colleagues-which begins with the statement that pending the conclusion ot a new commercial convention, with a view to which negotiations would begin immediately, the French and Canadian governments had agreed to "the following provisions". The leader of the Opposition is also aware that the French government called him to account for this engagement to begin immediately; and for reasons which I have not assailed, and which might have been good, he did not fulfil the terms of that engagement. Well, we have fulfilled the engagement of hon. gentlemen by entering into negotiations; and whether we had entered into such negotiations or not, we had notice that the French government would not continue the old arrangement. What, then, is the good of hon. gentlemen again and again quoting the existing rates as if they were at our disposal? They are not at our disposal. I say, they are dead and gone; and if we did not adopt this treaty, wise or unwise as it may be, fair or unfair, we should have to come under the operations of the French general tariff. A comparison between that tariff and this treaty is a fair matter; a comparison between the existing rates, which are 4 p.m. dead and gone, and the treaty before us is not a fair matter. Notwithstanding' the provisions of the preceding paragraphs, His Britannic Majesty will not be entitled to claim for raw materials or manufactured articles the produce of the territories of his Britannic Majesty the benefit of any special treatment which his Catholic Majesty has conceded or may concede to the products of Portugal or to those originating in and proceeding from the Spanish zone of Morocco.
In several other treaties the French are now inserting that provision. I admit that it is susceptible of the interpretation that my hon. friend suggests, but I am assured and believe that that is not really its main purpose; it is intended to deal chiefly with the matter of reparations. Belgium, for instance, is a neighbouring country; France may wish in connection with accounts between France and Belgium to bring in Belgian goods; and German goods may have to go into France by way of reparation. This arrangement is also contemplated by the Treaty of Versailles -that in the adjustments of commercial relations regard is to be had to the needs of France in the matter of reparations. I do not think there is any danger to be apprehended in that connection. Our real competitor in France is'the United States, and if we are assured of the most favoured nation treatment as respects that country I think we may reasonably be content. However, on that point my hon. friend was right; the clause is wider than I thought it was, but I am satisfied that it brings no harm.

speechtext:
My hon. friend has now given absolutely the strongest argument in favour of the treaty which has yet been advanced, namely that it can be got rid of in six months. I again ask the Finance Minister if under this contract with France, where the general tariff is 100 and the minimum tariff is 50 the latter could not be advanced to 90. Cannot France do that?
French Treaty

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The essence of these
clauses is that we get the same treatment as the United States. If France makes any such changes as my hon. friend describes and gives advantages to the United States she must also give them to Canada. That is the essence of the arrangement.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: What I want to know is whether France can do what I have suggested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: France might possibly do it but she would have to give the benefit to Canada as well as to the United States.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend is not following me. I will use this illustration : Suppose we have a general rate of 1,000 and a minimum rate of 500. Now then we will assume that the minimum rate is increased by 50 per cent which would bring that rate up to 750. Is there anything to prevent France from bringing that minimum up to 750 or even 900?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It could not be done
while the arrangement with the United States exists. If that arrangement terminates we have the assurance that we shall get the best terms that are going.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
France could
do it apart from that arrangement could it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It could.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It could do
that? So that that is the result. W'e would suffer that loss and practically get no advantage at all. I point out to my hon. friend the advantages enjoyed by France under article X and ask my hon. friend why it is that different treatment should be handed out to Canada. In article X it will be observed, France enjoys a discount of 10 per cent in addition to the benefit of the intermediate tariff. France retains any benefit she enjoys under the contract but the benefit which is granted to Canada may be taken from her. Why is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was something which pleased France and did not hurt us.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It does not
hurt Canada to get terms which are unfavourable to her and are favourable to France? Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is arguing the matter. I am not bound to agree with his argument.
fSir Henry Drayton.]

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: If any wrong is done to Canada under this contract I want to understand it. There is an absolute covenant in article X, as I understand it, that the proportionate difference between the intermediate and general tariffs shall at no time be less than it is at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is no provision of the like protecting Canada herself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is no like provision.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend says there is no like provision. Is there any provision which, although not of a like character, does protect Canada? If so I would like to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am afraid I will have to let my hon. friend proceed with his argument.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: The question at issue here is not the argument I am advancing, that is r'f'f what the committee should vote on. They must vote on what the government has to say about its own legislation. This is a government measure. Is there any clause, even if it is not of a like character, which gives any protection to Canada at all? If there is will the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries kindly point it out. I do not think there is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have told the hon. gentleman that there is no such covenant. I have told him that the explanation is that the French government attached importance to one thing, we did not attach great importance to it, and in the framing of a treaty you have got to try and please both sides. In this case it was something the French wanted; we did not think it was of any importance.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is no
clause granting similar protection to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: We shall see how the treaty works out. It must be judged by its results.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is a bit lopsided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Possibly.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend quite clear that we shall always get the same treatment as the United States? As I read the treaty if France gives greater concessions to the United States in the future than it is now giving to Canada we shall have to pay for those concessions, and the United States will not.

French Treaty

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have the guarantee that in the case of the goods mentioned in schedules A and B we will get as good treatment as the United States and that is what we think is the main feature. In A and B we think we have covered practically everything that we are likely to export-hon. gentlemen opposite think we have covered a great deal more-but everything we can reasonably expect to export is covered by A and B. As respects other articles, if later on something new arises and the United States gets some favoured privileges and we think we are entitled to get similar privileges in return for some fair concession the two governments have agreed, they will recognize that obligation and by mutual conference will come to an agreement. If France gives the United States some advantage they must give it to us for a fair return. That is only reasonable.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it reasonable under this contract that we should have to give concessions to France for advantages which are extended to the United States without any obligation on her part? I ask my hon. friend if that is reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not quite understand my hon. friend's question.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Let me read the article in question:
If at any time France grants to the United States of America for any products other than those enumerated in schedules A and B to this convention more favourable treatment than is granted to Canada, Canada shaill be entitled to claim the benefit of the same treatment for any identical or similar products originating in and coming from Canada, on condition that France shall be entitled to ask from Canada a reasonable and equivalent concession. France undertakes to give due consideration to any claim thus put forward by Canada and promptly to make known what concession of a similar nature she wishes to receive in return. The governments of the two countries undertake to examine these questions in a friendly spirit and with a mutual desire to arrive at an equitable agreement.
I point out' to my hon. friend that, under that reservation, valuable concessions can be granted to the United States for nothing, and that Canada has a right to get the same concessions, if she is able to make a new arrangement, a new treaty with France in connection with them, at the price of giving concessions of a similar, or some other nature. Perhaps I am wrong in saying of a similar nature. She has to give valuable considerations for further tariff rights or advantages in France which the United States may get for nothing. My hon. friends may think that is right, but I venture to think that it is not right, that in view of the tremendous amount
that is already being given, that we ought, as a matter of course, to get the benefit of any further concessions granted to the United States without giving any further concession. We must remember that we have given this long list. While we have surrendered our autonomy having regard to a great many items which are absolutely fixed, while we give this exact percentage of difference as between the intermediate and the general tariff, the United States has given nothing. Surely my hon. friend does not mean that if the United States, on top of all this, gets something further it is reasonable Canada should pay to get the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: The observations of my hon. friend may be well founded, perhaps, if he has the knowledge which his remarks would imply. In that case, however, I must compliment him on the fact that he possesses superior knowledge to that which I possess, because he tells us the United States are going to get something for nothing. How he knows the terms and conditions the French government are going to give the United States passes my comprehension; I confess I do not know. This agreement does not make any limitations as to the terms of any agreement between France and the United States. They can make their own arrangement. What is most likely to happen, I think, in view of events that are occurring at the present time, is that the present arrangement with the United States will not last long, and I have not any fear that they will get any terms or conditions not extended to Canada. This is not an agreement to determine what the United States and France will do, and the only relation of the United States is this: that if she is our chief competitor, and we take care that whatever France gives the United States in the matter of concessions she must give to us, I do not see anything wrong in that. I think it is reasonable, we have covered in A, and B, everything Canada wants to send to France. If it turns out there is something else, and France makes some arrangement with the United States, then she must give us the same terms, if it is something new. If the United States gets something new, what is unfair in saying that the representatives of France and the representatives of Canada may sit down and deal with it? France may say to us: "Well, we are giving this to the United States, and we will give it to you if you give us some concession in return". What is wrong in that? Nothing.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon friend did not get me. What I was pointing out
227S
French Treaty

was that we pay the price for what we are getting. The United States to-day has not paid the price for what she has got.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: The United States did not get that in our day; they got it while other gentlemen were managing public affairs, and we have no responsibility for it.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suppose the hon. minister thinks he assisted the United States in getting the contracts. I suppose he thinks we have something to do with the United States' people getting the contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: No I do not think so.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then, why did the minister make the remark?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend is introducing the United States in the matter; we are not doing so.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is really missing the point in this matter altogether. My hon. friends go over there and they find an existing condition of affairs. I am not dragging in the United States, this contract drags it in and my hon. friend drags it in. They say they want as good a deal as the United States. Very good. I point out to my hon. friend-and if I am wrong I want to be corrected, because I am only trying to get the truth in connection with this matter-that considerable trouble has been given by Canada in connection with this treaty. My hon. friend has said that this treaty puts Canada in the position of the United States, her chief competitor. These words were used by my hon. friend more than once during this debate. I point out to him that the United States paid nothing whatever for any of these things. If I am wrong I want to be corrected. I think I am right, and I point out that under this very contract that is the state of affairs which my hon. friend recognizes as proper, not only for the present but for the future. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) is a lawyer; I have no doubt he looked after the drafting of the treaty; one would naturally expect that. Well, under this clause which is drawn here, France may give-I do not say must give-so and so. My hon. friend seemed to know an awful lot about what France would do. I do not pretend to know. All I know is about this contract, which is supposed to look after Canada's interest. I point out to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that France may give further advantages to the United States in her market, and she may give them for nothing- there is nothing said one way or the other
fSir Henry Drayton.]
as to the terms of agreement between France and the United States. And I further say that the effect of this agreement is that, although the United States may have got those additional things covered by this contract for nothing, Canada is not to get them for nothing as the United States did, but has to pay a consideration for them. I will ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether that is not correct.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is wrong with the clause as it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This clause does not
purport to deal with the relations between France and the United States. If I could only get that into my hon. friend's head it would save him a lot of trouble. This is an agreement, whether wise or hot, between France and Canada. France and the United States can do anything they like in commercial matters. The only advantage is that in respect of a wide range of articles, if France is going to give certain concessions to the Uni ted States-and this list covers nearly everything we need-she must give those concessions to Canada and if something new arises, and she gives it to the United States, we can say to her "This is a new commodity. we have a right to it, let us sit down and arrange what we will give for it." I cannot see anything wrong in that. My hon. friends thought we were making an arrangement with the United States but we are not.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I never contended that this was a contract binding the United States. I was speaking simply of sections of this treaty, drafted, I suppose, by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe). I am not bringing into this contract anything that is not there now!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. gentleman is telling us that under this contract, the United States can do certain things. I say that this contract has nothing to do with the United States.
Sir HENRY I)R A) TON: My hon. friend is quite in error about that. This contract, as regards this particular matter that we are discussing, says that if France gives the United States further concessions, we are to get the same concessions, if we can make an agreement. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It says further that we are to give something for those concessions.

French Treaty

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Further concessions.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: On both sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, we are dealing only with the one side.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Are we not dealing with France and Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Are they not two ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Two sides?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: So, this is dealing with concessions on both sides. France makes concessions to the United States. Canada comes along and says: "I want those concessions from you." France says: "Give me so many more concessions," and that is the way the matter would be worked out. What I am poinitng out to the minister is that a treaty has been negotiated by France with both Canada and the United States, that while concessions are granted to the United States for nothing, a consideration is asked from Canada and that if further concessions are made to the United States we can only get equivalent concessions by paying for them. Am I overstating that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: We will under this treaty enjoy, not many, but some concessions that the United States do not get. Again I must ask my hon. friend to notice this. This is a contract, not between France and the United States, but between France and Canada. Recognizing, whether rightly or wrongly, the fact that the United States is our greatest competitor, surely we want to claim the best terms that are given to the United States. Therefore we put in that list B, which guarantees the best terms given to the United States, a long list of items which hon. members think are too many. We put in schedules A and B practically all articles that Canada is likely to want included, and we may say that if something more arises, we shall make a special arrangement about it. I cannot see anything wrong in that.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Except that again the United States gets something for nothing, and we pay. Apparently, however, we are not gaining anything by further discussion as to that. What is the effect in law, or what is the intended effect of article 17?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: A clause of that kind will be found in every commercial treaty between two nations. It is simply guaranteeing between the two nations that they will have the same privileges as regards interior transit and so forth. I do not think there is anything new in it.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: The sales tax is something that is new since the old commercial treaty was made. What is the view of the government in connection with the sales tax, considering articles 17 and 18?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Both France and Canada have at present local taxes which, we think, balance one another, and I do not think there is going to be trouble on that score. It means that, practically speaking, there shall be mutual guarantee of equal treatment in these things. If the cost of applying these things seems to be a large matter, that might be a subject of negotiation. I think, however, there will be no trouble in regard to it. Our sales tax on the one hand and the French local tax on the other will balance one another.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that the point is covered or that he does not fear trouble?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think it is covered.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under the contract what is my hon. friend's view as to the sales tax on French goods coming into Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: We will treat the goods of France the same as we treat the goods of any other foreign country.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is that national treatment; is that the way in which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries understood it; or when he was drawing that contract and advising the Minister of Finance in regard to the legal effect of it, is this not what he thought, that he w'as going to give the goods of France the same treatment as the goods of Canada, once he had exacted his lower duties?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What my hon. friend refers to is the last clause of article 18, which reads:
Subject to the laws now in force in either country France and Canada grant each other national treatment as regards consumption dues or other duties imposed upon the sale of goods.
The sales tax will apply to French goods in this country.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I thank my hon friend for reading the clause. I was asking what it meant.
French Treaty

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend has done nothing this afternoon but read from the treaty.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have been asking the hon. member what he meant by certain sections. What does this section mean?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It means what it says. It is very clear.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does it mean that France and Canada agree with each other that the products of France in Caanda and the products of Canada in France shall both be subject to like treatment?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: To the laws in force in France and in Canada.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is hardly an answer to my question. Are they both to be subject to like treatment under those laws?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: We cannot adjust the laws in France and Canada so as to be the same on everything.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I really credited my hon. friend with more intelligence.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I cannot say that of my hon. friend after some of the remarks he has macle.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: On the terms of his considered clause, can the extra sales tax charged on imported articles be charged on articles coming from France?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: The extra sales tax over the Canadian-can that be done?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under what section?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Section 18.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Has an opinion been received from the Department of Justice on that question?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely national treatment means that what is charged on Canadian goods shall be charged on French goods. It is so clear.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that is not the point. Does he not know-

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know that is what you are talking about all the time. '

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does he not know there is a difference-

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not think you do.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend not know that there is a difference in the rate on imported articles and on domestic articles?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, we want to have this matter cleared up; we want to know what stand the government is going to take. In this contract Canada covenants with France to give France certain treatment in her markets, and we want to know whether, over and above the tariff duties reserved by the contract, the government can also charge a rate of sales tax on the imported goods of France, as of other countries, higher than the rate she levies on her own goods. We want to know what stand the government takes in this matter, and I think we are entitled to the information. In view of the covenant of the treaty, does the government concede that this internal tax of ours, the sales tax, is to apply to goods imported from France?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Read the concluding
words of the article.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: But I want the government's position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I cannot undertake to explain it more clearly than it is stated in the act; I am not a lawyer. It seems that my hon. friend wishes to continue the discussion and I think we had better call it six o'clock. However, I shall not be able to be here this evening and I ask that the committee report progress.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before we rise I will ask the minister to get some information in regard to item 214 in schedule B. This item refers to wheels, tires and wheel centres of iron or steel. I want to know what kind of tires this refers to, whether of steel or rubber?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY CONVENTION CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall get the information.
Progress reported.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Definition of "opium joint" repealed:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 1 and clause 2 will have for effect to strike out the criminal code provisions with regard to opium joints as it is considered that this subject is more satisfactorily covered by the provisions of sections 4, 10, 11 and 12 of Bill No. 72, an "Act to prohibit the improper use of opium and other drugs," which passed the House the other day. On section 3-Amendment to penalty clause in respect to advertising, printing, posting or selling intelligence on horse-races:
Would the minister give us an explanation of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have already given an explanation to the House. This prohibits advertisements and the printing and publishing, exhibiting and giving of tips, selections and odds on horse-races. Reading the clause, which is very clear, the House will find that we propose that in the future no one shall be permitted to advertise, print, publish, exhibit, post up, sell or supply, or offer to sell or supply:
(i)	other than on the premises of an association lawfully conducting race meetings in Canada, and during the actual progress of a race meeting thereon, any tips, selections, odds, winning money prices, pari-mutuel payments, or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to any horse-race, whether such race be held within or without the Dominion of Canada, and whether at the time of advertising, printing, publishing, exhibiting, posting up or applying such news or information such race has or has not taken place;
The second part of the section reads as follows:
(ii)	any information intended to assist in or intended for use in connection with book-making, pool-selling, betting or wagering upon any fight, game, sport or race, other than a horse-race whether at the time of advertising, printing, publishing, exhibiting, posting up or supplying such news or information, such fight, game, sport or race has or has not taken place.
That is to say that no publicity as to betting, book-making and pool selling on horseraces will be allowed in any other place or at any other time than on the race-track during a race. By the second part of the section this will apply to all cases of betting on games * or races of any kind.

Criminal Code

I think, perhaps, we should have some little further explanation as to why betting should be permitted during the time of a race on the race-track and made illegal at all other times; as to why a monopoly should be given in the matter of betting on horse-races at the time of a race meeting and should not be extended to other kinds of betting in other places. I do not quite see the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This point was debated and disposed of by the House at a previous sitting. The pari-mutuel system was discussed and the House by a large majority decided that it should be retained. Betting on horse-races was also considered at the same time, and it would seem that the opinion of the House was in favour of its being allowed. The great abuse, as to which we have received complaints, is not the betting on race-tracks but the betting outside, and especially the book-making and the pool-selling not only on races in Canada but on races outside of the Dominion. I am afraid that the prohibition of betting on race-tracks, as it has obtained for years past, would have the result of creating difficulties.
Under this provision is it not impossible for a man to enjoy the practice of betting except on a race-track and during the time of the meeting?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The betting is only allowed on the race-track. It has been so for many years.
Does that not give a monopoly of the betting to those who are conducting the horse-races?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not necessarily.
Anyone can bet on a race-track; everyone is free to do so.

In the case of a
baseball game does betting become illegal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; that is to say the advertising of it.
Is it illegal to bet on a baseball game while the game is in progress?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a private game you can bet any amount you like. What we want to do is to prohibit the book-making and the pool-selling on any games. In the case of horse-races betting is only allowed on the track during the course of the meeting.

I think there was an amendment proposed last year if not to this section perhaps to section 236-a section at least allied [DOT] 
to this one, and relating to guessing contests conducted by certain newspapers. I think the minister was asked some time ago if, in view of the decisions which had been recorded in the courts, it was the intention of the government to bring in an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will bring it in
immediately after this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I now beg to propose that the following section be' added to the bill:
Section 412 of the said act is amended by inserting the word "badge" after the word "ticket" in the second line thereof and also after the word "ticket" in the third line thereof.
The amendment is asked for by the Toronto Transportation Commission, and appears to be unobjectionable. Section 412 provides that everyone is guilty of an indictable offence ana liable to six months' imprisonment who by means of any false ticket or order, or of any other ticket or order, fraudulently and unlaw-

Criminal Code
fully obtains or attempts to obtain passage on any carriage, tramway or railway, or in any steam or other vessel. The effect of the amendment is to extend these provisions to the fraudulent use of a badge as well as a ticket or order.
Amendment agreed to.

I move that the following section be added to the bill:-
Section 1024A of the said act as enacted by chapter 43 of the statutes of 1920, is amended by inserting after the word "conviction" in the fourth line thereof the words "or acquittal".
This is the case my hon. friend for Calgary (Mr. Shaw) had in mind.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 1024A was adpoted in 1920, Chapter 43 of 10-11 George V and reads:
Either the attorney general of the province, or any person convicted of an indictable offence, may appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada from the judgment of any Court of Appeal setting aside or confirming a conviction for an indictable offence if it conflicts with the judgment of any other Court of Appeal in like case.
I have the following memorandum on the subject:
This amendment is asked for by the Attorney General of Alberta, and appears to me to be unobjectionable. As section 1024A stands at present (1920, chap. 43, sec. 16), it does not? cover the case of a person acquitted in the court below, and the purpose of the amendment is to make it extend to such a case. It appears that in the case of Rex. v. Stubbs, 24 Ca. Cr. Cas. page 303, the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Alberta decided that a certain kind of automatic gum vending machine, which paid rewards or premiums of varying amounts upon irregularly occurring times, was not a gambling device under section 228 of the code, whereas it has been held unanimously by the Courts of Appeal of both Ontario and Quebec that the machine in question is a gambling device, and this has also been held by the Court of Appeal of Manitoba. In the case of one MacNeil, subsequent to the Stubbs case, the Appellate Court of Alberta unanimously held that notwithstanding the decision of the Appellate Courts of the other provinces above mentioned they were not prepared to overrule their decision in the Stubbs case. The result is that the law of Alberta on this subject is not the same as that of the other provinces, and as the purpose of section 1024A was to provide a means of obtaining uniformity of interpretation of the Criminal Code throughout all the provinces, I think the section should be amended as above so as to cover cases like the Stubbs case.
That is to say, that under a special section of the Criminal Code the Appellate Courts of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba have decided that a certain machine was a gambling machine. The Appellate Court of Alberta has decided the contrary. To make sure what the real meaning of any clause of our Criminal Code is it was provided in 1920 that in such cases where decisions were contradictory, an appeal should be provided to the Supreme Court, so that the citizens of Canada might be sure as to the meaning of any of the sections of our Criminal Code. As the section was drafted, it only applied to conviction on appeal to set aside a conviction, and did not apply to the case of acquittal, so that in case of acquittal the attorney general or any other interested party had not the right to appeal. By adding the words "or acquittal" the whole case will be covered.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think this was the amendment my hon. friend for Calgary West intended to introduce.

The point I had in mind was in connection with some legislation passed last year. My recollection is that it was an amendment to section 235 or 236 of the code. The legislation introduced dealt with what were commonly known as guessing contests, conducted by newspapers, and based upon the results of football and baseball games and sports of that character. Apparently in most of the western cities, at least, means have been found to get around the provisions of the statutes, and I was simply inquiring from the Minister of Justice as to whether he proposed to amend that section since the act was passed last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does the last part of subsection (f) not cover the case?
(f) Any information intended to assist or intended for use in connection with bookmaking, pool selling, betting upon any track, game, sport or race.

I am afraid that would not cover the case. The minister is probably familiar with the legislation. It apparently * originated in the Senate last year. It is a guessing contest depending upon the result of football or baseball games, the newspaper charging a small amount for each guess, and then paying a very large amount, usually dependent upon the number of subscribers, to those who guess most nearly the results of these events. I have not had time to consider this amendment, but I think it only deals with information supplied for a particular purpose and does not deal with the actual contest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The actual contest is the game. The amendment applies to all games, except horse-races.

It seems to me there should be a protest against this class of legislation. I for one do not want to do anything that will encourage betting or gambling.
Canada Temperance Act

But I cannot see why certain exceptions ' should be made and others should be penalized for carrying on what is precisely the same kind of thing. There are certain men who bet on a horse race on the tracks, and apparently that is perfectly legal. Other men who seem to want to exercise the same right, whether it is good, bad or indifferent, and to do some betting, are immediately performing an illegal act. This thing was brought to my attention last year in connection with some of these papers that were carrying on guessing contests of this character. I am free to admit that personally I do not like this kind of thing; but these people who are doing this kind of thing are perfectly justified in protesting that if it is right for one group in the community to be allowed the privilege of betting, it is right for other groups in the community to be allowed the same privilege, and there ought not to be discriminatory legislation of this kind.

Section agreed to.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Radiotelegraph Act, chapter forty-three of the statutes of 1913, by providing that the Governor in Council may authorize the payment of a portion of the license fees collected in respect of certain prescribed licenses, to a provincial government, private company, or other prescribed party, and notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any act, to any department or employee thereof, for services given in connection with the operation of broadcasting stations and for services performed for the minister in connection with the licensing and inspection of stations.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Section 10 of the present act gives to the Governor in Council the right
to prescribe the tariff of fees to be paid for

Radiotelegraph Act
licenses and for examination for certificates of proficiency held and issued under the provisions of the act. This amendment relates to radiotelephone broadcasting stations. During the past two years considerable progress has been made in the development of radiotelegraphy, and whereas last year there were issued about ten thousand licenses for receiving stations it is estimated that during the present year the .number will be increased to about fifty thousand. These receiving stations are served by broadcasting stations that are rather expensive to maintain. Last year there were forty broadcasting stations but only twenty-five have renewed their licenses for this year. The cost of a broadcasting station varies from 87,000 to $20,000 and the maintenance cost from $2,000 to $5,000 or $6,000 a year. At present these broadcasting stations are operated either by the vendors of apparatus or by newspapers and big de-. partmental stores for advertising purposes, and also by a provincial government and private companies. In Ottawa there is a broadcasting station operated by Mr. Booth. As I say, the upkeep is rather expensive and this bill proposes to meet the case of Manitoba, among others. In that province there were two broadcasting stations in Winnipeg operated by the Winnipeg Free Press and the Winnipeg Tribune, both of which have closed down. The Manitoba government however now operates a telephone line in the province and it is quite prepared to establish and maintain a first class broadcasting station; but the authorities want to have some remuneration. It is therefore deemed- advisable that part of the license fee should be given to these broadcasting stations which serve the public. After all, they are affording enjoyment to thousands of listeners and it is only fair that they should receive some remuneration for their services. It is also provided that part of the license 9 p.m. fee should be given for the services rendered the minister in connection with the licensing and inspection of stations. It is the intention to have the Manitoba government, or any other corporation with which the department may enter into an arrangement for the purpose, issue licenses on behalf of the department, for which they will be paid part of the license fee as remuneration for their services in collecting the fees for this government. The same thing applies to inspection; if they provide inspectors they will be paid part of the license fee for the purpose. I believe this is the best arrangement that could be made, and it is to that end that the bill is proposed.
I suppose we shall have an opportunity of discussing the matter in detail when the bill is brought down?
As my hon. friend desires; but really there is not much either in the resolution or in the bill.

It would be of interest to the House to know who are operating broadcasting stations at present. The minister might also tell us what proportion of the fee he proposes to give to the stations. Is the act going to define that?

It will be fixed by regulation.

I think my hon. friend is wrong when he says there is no change from the present act. It is true thai under order in council the amount of the fes is fixed, but that must be a flat level; no differentiation can be made. In the present case a portion of the fee is to be paid to the broadcasting station. What I want to know is whether that amount will be at the minister's discretion or whether there is to be a regular rule regarding the matter?
There will be a regular rule. I am of opinion myself that the same proportion of the fee should go for the same services rendered anywhere in Canada.

Does the minister think that he should help reduce the cost of advertisers by refunds of this kind? I notice from the list he has read that a great many of the people operating these stations are using them really only to advertise their business. Does he propose to help them to carry the cost of that advertising?

I am sure their intention is to advertise their business. Still, they are giving concerts, lectures and so on, and thus contributing to the enjoyment of the receivers. There may be something in my hon. friend's suggestion, but my present impression is that it would be hard to differentiate.

Take the case of broadcasting, which is entirely for the purpose of selling radio instruments and parts. Does the minister intend, in effect, to help to carry the cost of selling this equipment by contributing a part of the license fee?

These matters will all have to be considered; all we ask is the power of regulation. There may be a difference between a purely philanthropic company organized only for the purpose of giving enjoyment to the thousands of listeners, and a company which broadcasts chiefly for its own benefit.

Complaints come from the receivers with regard to the tremendous misuse of broadcasting, resulting in conflict of currents, and the like. Has the minister considered that question at all?
Mr. LAPOINTE. Yes. The reason for the collection of the fee is to pay for the services of inspectors to prevent that very thing.
What are the regulations in that respect? I have not noticed anything in the statute that would cover it. How does the minister now police broadcasting?
We have inspectors all over Canada, seven on the permanent staff and twenty-eight on part time.

What are the
regulations which govern broadcasting?
I have not the regulations here; if my hon. friend desires to have them I can furnish them. I do not see, however, that it is necessary to have them for the purposes of this legislation.

If the general interest is considered, it is that of the receivers rather than that of the transmitters. I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but I am told that the receiver does not interfere with the currents, so that the receiver is not to blame for all these difficulties. It is the sender, the broadcaster who is responsible for that. Am I not right?

The trouble my hon. friend refers to arises in connection with the operations of transmitting stations of which there are 1,900 throughout Canada. It is the duty of the inspectors, among other things, to see that these stations do not get off what they call the wave-length and thus interfere with broadcasting. The transmitting stations are different from the broadcasting stations.
But there is conflict even on the part of the main broadcasting station themselves. Upon whom are the fees placed, upon the broadcaster and the transmitter, or upon those who listen?

The fee payable by the receivers is only one dollar per year. The broadcasting stations have to pay 850 per year. In Great Britain the license fee for the receiving stations is $2.50; and they are proceeding on the same basis as that on which we want to proceed. Of that fee of $2.50, one-half goes to the department and one-half to the broadcasting company. This system has been in operation only since December last. There are over 100,000 licenses for receiving stations in England.
I hope the result will not be the multiplication of broadcasting, because the chief trouble to-day is that there is so much conflict in the waves. Is the service self-supporting?

Not yet.

speechtext: This section was allowed to stand with the consent of the committee.

The bill as originally presented met with the entire approval of the authors but met with very much opposition from the printers and publishers. The committee will

Copyright Act

remember that when this bill was before the House a few days ago, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), presented considerable opposition to this section that is now under consideration. I have had a. conference with my hon. friend and have submitted to him an amendment which we hope will meet with the approval of both the authors and the printers and publishers, but I am bound to confess that to-night I am somewhat confused to find that my hon. friends opposite, who I thought were opposed to our bill as originally presented, now seem to indicate that they might be opposed to the amendment I had in mind to present to satisfy those whom my hon. friend for South Wellington represents. I am bound to say on behalf of the government that if the committee is willing, the government would be quite prepared to allow the bill to go through as originally presented, but my hon. friend for South Wellington presented an argument the other evening which almost convinced me that there were others who had some rights, and I was hoping that the amendment would satisfy all interested.

I must say that I have been taking no stand at all on the bill or the proposed amendment. I was simply asking for information, and I have not been given any information yet as to what the minister thinks of this telegram or as to what is going to be done. Perhaps it would be fair to ask the minister just what is being done by this bill. What rights are being created on the one hand, and what rights are being taken away on the other, either from the publishers or authors?

Perhaps my hon. friend for
South Wellington would present his argument again to the House.

I would think the government would have some idea of what they were about. I would think that the minister ought to be able to tell the House what he thinks should be done. He tells us that there was an argument made against the bill the other day by the hon. member for South Wellington, but it does seem to me that the responsible minister in charge of a highly important bill like this should tell the House just exactly whose rights the bill will interfere with on the one hand, and what rights it will create on the other, and generally what the effect of the legislation is.

Perhaps my hon. friend was not in the House when the bill was presented a few days ago. Had he been here
[Mr. Robb.)
then he would have known that not onlv the hon. member for South Wellington but the chief whip of the Opposition, the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) presented considerable opposition to this particular clause. My hon. friend will remember that the government of which he was a member put through a Copyright Act in 1921, which was assented to on the 4th of June, 1921, but after having passed both Houses of Parliament the government for reasons which I am not called upon to explain never proclaimed the act although they were in power all the balance of that year. It was contended that the act passed in 1921 failed to comply with the requirements of the Berne convention, and that consequently Canadian authors were deprived of privileges which they might otherwise enjoy. This amendment now presented to the House is to make the bill of 1921 acceptable to the authorities of the Berne convention and to allow Canada to become a member of that convention.

Has the minister been able to find any correspondence with the Berne convention to show that the convention itself objects to those particular clauses of the act of 1921? I might say that I made the statement when the bill was before the House on a former occasion that information had come to me that the only objection that had been made by the Berne convention was an article which appeared in a newspaper published in Switzerland which is supposed to be the official or unofficial organ of the Copyright convention. I stated that my opinion was that the article had been written by a civil servant in Ottawa, and that that was the only objection which the Swiss authorities had so far taken. Since that time the gentleman whom I have named, the member of the Civil Service, has done me the honour of calling upon me and explaining that the article in question which appeared in the newspaper in Switzerland was not actually written by him. He says he supplied the material and the records to the newspaper, but did not actually write the article. I think in justice to this gentleman named I should make that statement to the committee. While I am on my feet permit to say this: I was satisfied when the bill was up before, and I am just as firmly satisfied now that apart from the minister himself there is not a man in the committee at this present moment who understands this legislation
You might include me.

And the minister himself admits that I may include him. I have tried

Copyright Act
to get to the bottom of this matter; I have spent a lot of time on it and I confess I do not fully understand it now. My suggestion to the minister, when the bill was last up, was that he appoint a small committee, as was done in 1921, before whom the authors, publishers and printers can appear and state their claims. The committee will have to go to the bottom of the matter and report on this bill. I understood that my suggestion on that occasion agreed with the view of the minister. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) backed up the proposal very emphatically. He said that he did not understand it, that the committee did not either, and he refused to commit himself to legislation which he did not understand. I do not know any-[DOT] thing quite as complicated or quite as involved as the coypright question. I do know this, however: In 1921 a special committee was appointed, the various interested parties were heard, and they agreed on the legislation then passed. The bill was passed but it was not proclaimed because under the peculiar situation which exists, as between Dominion laws and Imperial laws, it was necessary, or at all events it was deemed proper, to submit the legislation before proclamation to the Imperial authorities, because they reserved the right to proclaim our act in the London Gazette which is the official communication between Great Britain and the Berne convention. The bill was not proclaimed.
The minister says that intimation has come from the authorities of the British government that the particular provisions mentioned in section 3 are objectionable, that they are not in conformity with either the letter or the spirit of the Imperial act. Well, that is rather an old complaint in regard to copyright by the Imperial government. In 1910 when the late Sydney Fisher was minister he attended an Imperial conference upon this very question. An agreement was then reached between the Imperial authorities and the authorities of the various dominions represented at that conference, and the Imperial act of 1911 was passed which practically recognized the agreement that was then come to. So far as I can understand the Imperial legislation of 1911 and the act passed by this parliament in 1921, I do not see that we have come in conflict in any way with the Imperial act, nor do I believe that we have in any way come in conflict with the Berne convention. The authors and writers in Canada say we have. I do not see in what respect we have come in contact. The publishers and printers in Canada say we have not. They desire to
146}
have the act passed in 1921 put in force. The minister intimated when this bill was last discussed that he would produce a communication the department had received from the British government. I have not had the opportunity of seeing that communication, nor do I know just what the objection of the Imperial government is. It was stated that the copyright convention had made objection. My information is that it has not done so; but objection had been taken at the instance of a certain civil servant who had sent forward the article referred to for publication in Switzerland.
I am now going to renew my request to the minister that he appoint a special committee to consider this bill. I have said all that I can say on that subject. I know there is a great deal more to be learned on the subject than I know; there is a great deal more to be said than I have said. If the government, take the responsibility of passing this bill-they have a majority and can do so-they will only do it over my protest. Again I ask that the minister, who admits he does not know the substance of the Copyright Act or what the effect of the amendment will be, let this bill go to a special committee. He has handed me the draft of an amendment wihch has been prepared since the matter was last before the House. I think it is a decided improvement on the bill which he introduced. I am neither going to consent to it-I have no power to do so-nor am I going to oppose it. But if this bill goes through in the form in which it has been introduced, or in the shape in which the minister wants it, he must take the responsibility. I know the publishers all object to it, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association objeftt to it. and the printing trades throughout Canada object to it. Those in favour of the bill are apparently the authors or writers of the country. Their reason for supporting this legislation is this:	If this bill, or if the
amendment to the act of 1921 passes, it will not be necessary for writers to have their books published in Canada; they can publish them in the United States and avoid publication in this country. Under the law passed in 1921 where an author publishes his work in the United States provision was made for publication in Canada on payment to the author of the exact royalty or fee which he received from the American publisher. If the author would not agree to that then the publisher had the right to go to the Secretary of State, I think it was, or to the commissioner and get a license for the publication of
Copyright Act

that work in Canada on payment to the author of the exact amount which he received for his work in the United States. That arrangement seemed to me to be pretty fair. That is the arrangement, I am informed, which was agreed to in 1921 before the bill was passed.
The United States does not belong to the copyright convention. The United States insists that anybody who gets copyright in that country shall publish there, otherwise you will get no copyright. A Canadian author is therefore in this position: There is a market for his literary work in the shape of 120,000,000 of English speaking people, it is the greatest book-buying population in the world. Naturally the Canadian writer wishes to sell his work and to get copyright in that market. He is bound to have publication there and when he sells the American rights he sells the Canadian rights as well. The American publisher then says "I am not going to publish in Canada, I will publish in the United States," and it has been objected that very often there is no publication in this country. Sometimes it is said that there has not been a supply even of the works of the author in this country. Now, the publishers of Canada ask merely the right to republish in this country on payment to the author of the same amount that he receives from the American publisher. It looks fair to me but the authors do not agree to it. They ask that the bill passed in 1921 be amended in that respect by striking out the four clauses in question. On the other hand the publishers and the printers desire the act passed in 1921 to remain as it is, in order that the book publication and printing be done in this country and, they say, without any loss whatever tQ the author. That is the case as I understand it.
There is this other point: My view is that we should stick to our act passed in 1921. If the Imperial government has objection to make to that act let us know upon what the objection is based, let us understand what the objection is. I am satisfied that we should allow the act of 1921 to stand or to be proclaimed in the form in which it was then enacted. If objection is taken by the Imperial authorities we will know of it at once. The Prime Minister, I believe, is going to the Imperial conference in October next. He would be in a position then to discuss this matter with the Imperial authorities and see what the foundation of this objection is. The Prime Minister himself happens to be one of the authors of this country, and would be a person specially informed and specially 
qualified to discuss the question with the Imperial authorities.
My suggestion to the minister-rand it is only a suggestion-is that he drop his present bill and allow the act passed in 1921, after all parties had agreed to it, to be proclaimed. If the Imperial government objects, and says there is some way we have contravened their jurisdiction, that is a matter for further discussion between the authorities of the Imperial government and the Dominion government. I do not think there is any conflict over the jurisdiction of the Imperial government, or in regard to the rules and regulations of the Berne convention. I think the act passed in 1921 is strictly within our rights. I may be wrong in that, as I do not profess to be any kind of an expert in regard to copyright questions or copyright laws, but I would advise the minister to take one of two courses: either let the bill go to a special committee, and let that committee study the question, or withdraw the bill and let the act of 1921 be proclaimed. It will not take long to have the question settled, because the conference is meeting in October next, and it will probably deal with the matter and settle it. I think it is hopeless to ask the committee of the whole House to consider so intricate and involved a question as this, when I think, on the confession of everybody, including myself, we do not know the real principles at stake. We do not really understand the rules and regulations of the Berne convention or the attitude of the Imperial government, and I think it would be well to have this matter cleared up before the House attempts any further legislation.

The position of the minister reminds me of the position that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) found himself in last year. Of course, there is a little difference. The Minister of Agriculture-and I think, perhaps, this was the first time any responsible minister in this House ever did such a thing-introduced and carried through a bill which he characterized as a "rotten" bill. It was awful, as the min-
Copyright Act

ister said; nevertheless he put it through. I do not, however, think any other
10 p.m. responsible minister in a responsible parliament ever before admitted that he did not know anything about a bill, admitted the statement made on the floor of this House by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who has had to leave, that the minister himself, who was supposed to know something about the bill, knew nothing about it and yet asked this House, that is supposed to act intelligently, to have some knowledge of the subject, more than that, to be able to get a definite statement from the minister as to the effect of his legislation, to put this legislation through. I canot think my hon. friend is serious in his proposition.	.
I have told my hon. friend what the effect is.

All the minister has done in connection with it is to produce a letter that is merely a comment from the British authorities. The minister distinctly told the committee ten minutes or a quarter of an hour ago that he himself did not understand this bill. The hon. member f .*r South Wellington said that he was sure that no one in this House including himself understood it, and if there is now in the House any hon. gentleman who understands this bill, I should like him to stand up and say so. Then the minister himself says that he can be included in that description. Is it not a farce to ask the committee to pass the bill under those circumstances. The responsibility is on the government. There is nothing more that we can say or do.
